newsitem.title: DUBAI: Shipping lines say delays at Saudi's busiest port.
newsitem.headline: Shipping lines say delays at Saudi's busiest port.

text.p: Shipping lines and agents on Sunday complained of long delays at Saudi Arabia's busiest container port in Jeddah, saying the setbacks were prompting some lines to consider introducing container surcharges.
Speaking by telephone from the Red Sea city, shipping executives said there had been major delays since the October change in management of the port's container terminal.
"The problem is with the new contractor. They are having serious teething problems and have little experience," said one executive, referring to the new contractor, Gulf Stevedoring.
In October it took over the contract from Marine Terminals International, which had run the port for the past 18 years.
A Gulf Stevedoring official denied there were any delays and said the port was operating "beautifully".
"No, there is no delay at all," said Abdulghani Baksha, assistant general manager of operations of the port, which he said handles nearly one million containers a year.
A shipping manager said there were still delays, but they were not as severe as those suffered in Gulf Stevedoring's early days.
"They are trying their best and they have had a meeting with shipping lines and agents. It is better than it was in the beginning, but it is still not satisfactory," he said.
Jeddah shipping sources said some lines had last week suggested a $100 surcharge on standard container units leaving Jeddah due to the delays.
"Nobody has implemented it yet. It has not filtered through to the agents or customers yet," said one.

"There are an awful lot of problems at Jeddah. The surcharge plans are the latest in a string of developments. There was some storm damage, but basically since the new contractors there has been a slowdown," said the manager of a large European line.
"They have had a serious run of bad luck," he added, referring to Gulf Stevedoring staff and communication problems.

A shipping manager said some lines were considering bypassing Jeddah for Jordan's Aqaba port, while another said some lines had suspended loading export containers to avoid rising costs related to the delays.

"Most lines are not picking up export boxes because they can't afford to wait around to load them. We have been sending smaller ships from time to time to pick them up," said the manager of a large shipping agent in the harbour.
Some ships were waiting up to two days to come alongside the wharf, compared to a previous average two hours, executives said. Unloading containers was also taking much longer.
"There are an average 12 container moves an hour per crane from at least 18 previously. Often they are also using only one crane per ship, when they used to use two," said one.
But Baksha said they were an average 20 moves an hour.
